lead: The first reading brings us to the night of the Passover: the lamb without blemish, the blood on the doorposts, the meal eaten in haste with sandals on the feet, and God’s promise, “When I see the blood, I will pass over you.” In the Gospel the disciples of Jesus pluck grain on the sabbath, and Jesus answers the objection with Scripture: God desires mercy and not sacrifice, and the Son of Man is lord of the sabbath. Both readings are about a feast and the meaning of keeping it: the Passover is a memorial that rescues, and the sabbath is a gift that serves life. Today is also the optional memorial of Our Lady of Mount Carmel; the readings of the Friday are kept.

r.h: When I see the blood, I will pass over you
set: Nine plagues have fallen on Egypt, and Pharaoh has refused to let Israel go. Chapter 11 closes with the summary of verse 10: Moses and Aaron have done all the wonders, and Pharaoh’s heart remains hard. Then comes the tenth announcement, the death of the firstborn, and the instructions for the Passover. These instructions are given before the event, so that Israel may keep the night every year for ever. The book of Exodus is written to be remembered and re-lived in worship.
str: 11:10: the summary: the wonders were done, but Pharaoh’s heart stayed hard.
12:1–2: the Lord gives the instructions in Egypt; this month will be the first month of the year.
12:3–10: the lamb, chosen on the tenth day, kept until the fourteenth, killed at twilight and eaten roasted with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.
12:11–13: how to eat it, hurriedly and ready to travel; the Lord will pass through Egypt; the blood on the houses is the sign.
12:14: the day is to be a remembrance and a festival for all generations.
kw: The name of the feast. Its root is explained here as God “passing over” the houses with the blood (v. 13); it may also carry the sense of protecting.
The word used for any offering to God. The lamb must be whole and perfect; Christian tradition sees in it the image of Christ.
In the Bible to remember is not only to think but to make present again. The Jewish family at table still says that each generation is to see itself as brought out of Egypt.
vv: The Bible says both that Pharaoh hardened his own heart (8:15, 32) and that the Lord hardened it. The Hebrew way of speaking sees God’s hand even in the working out of human refusal. Pharaoh is never presented as a puppet; he is responsible for his choices.
Your lamb shall be without blemish, a year-old male;
The best is given. The family does not give what it can spare but a lamb of the first quality, and it keeps it from the tenth day, so that it comes to know it.
your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand;
The meal is a night of departure. Those who eat are already on the road, ready to leave a land of slavery.
when I see the blood, I will pass over you,
The blood on the doorposts is a sign of faith and obedience, and God’s promise is attached to the sign. The people are saved by God’s mercy through what he has told them to do.
This day shall be a day of remembrance for you.
The Passover is not only an event of the past but a feast. In keeping it Israel has remembered its liberation in every generation.
ch: From the New Testament onward the Church has read this night in the light of Christ. Paul says, “Christ, our paschal lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7), and John presents Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). The Catechism teaches that by celebrating the Last Supper with the apostles during the Passover meal Jesus gave the Jewish Passover its definitive meaning (CCC 1340), and that the Eucharist is the memorial in which his Passover becomes present (CCC 1363–1364). The Church honors the Jewish people, who have kept this feast through every century, and says of them that they are beloved by God for the sake of the fathers (Nostra Aetate 4).

r.h: I desire mercy and not sacrifice
set: Chapter 12 begins a series of conflicts over the sabbath. Jesus is walking through the grainfields with his disciples. The law of Moses allowed a traveler to pluck ears of grain by hand in a neighbor’s field (Deuteronomy 23:25), but forbade harvesting on the sabbath (Exodus 34:21). The question raised by some Pharisees is therefore a real one: is this plucking a kind of reaping? The debate is a debate within Judaism about how best to honor the sabbath; Jesus and the Pharisees both loved it. Jesus does not deny the sabbath but shows what it is for.
str: vv. 1–2: the hungry disciples pluck grain; some Pharisees object.
vv. 3–4: first answer: David and his companions, hungry, ate the bread of the Presence.
vv. 5–6: second answer: the priests work on the sabbath in the Temple and are blameless; something greater than the Temple is here.
vv. 7–8: Hosea 6:6: mercy over sacrifice; the Son of Man is lord of the sabbath.
kw: Twelve loaves set before the Lord in the sanctuary each sabbath, for the priests alone to eat (Leviticus 24:5–9). David took it for his hungry men when he fled (1 Samuel 21:1–6).
Hosea’s word ḥesed means loyal love, the faithful kindness that God shows and asks of his people. Matthew’s Greek eleos renders it.
The sabbath is God’s gift. Jesus claims for himself, as Son of Man, authority over the day that belongs to God.
vv: they began to pluck heads of grain and to eat.
The disciples are hungry, and the need is real. Jesus does not treat hunger as a small thing.
something greater than the temple is here.
In the sabbath debate, Jesus declares that with him the greatest holy thing is present: he is the place where God dwells with his people.
I desire mercy and not sacrifice
Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6, as he did in 9:13. Hosea does not reject sacrifice; he says that sacrifice without love misses its purpose.
the Son of Man is lord of the sabbath.
The sabbath was made for human beings, as Mark adds (Mark 2:27). The one who is Lord of the sabbath is the one who knows best how to keep it.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus never fails to respect the holiness of the sabbath, but gives it its authentic and divine meaning: “the sabbath was made for man”; Christ is the Lord of the sabbath (CCC 2173). Because the Lord rose on the first day, Christians keep the Lord’s Day, and the Church asks that works of charity and rest from unnecessary work mark the day (CCC 2184–2186). The Church has always seen that mercy is not opposed to worship but is its fruit. St Augustine is often quoted as teaching that true sacrifice is every work done to unite us to God in holy fellowship (City of God 10.6, in substance).

qa: How are we to read the death of the firstborn of Egypt?

It is a hard text, and we should not read it lightly. The book of Wisdom reads it as an answer to Pharaoh’s decree to kill the infants of Israel (Wisdom 18:5; compare Exodus 1:22). The Church takes no joy in anyone’s death, and the Passover tradition itself carries sorrow: in the Jewish Passover meal a little wine is spilled for each plague, remembering the suffering of the Egyptians. The text tells us above all that God will not let oppression stand and that he saves his people.
rite: The optional memorial of Our Lady of Mount Carmel recalls the Carmelite family, which took its name from Mount Carmel in the Holy Land, where the prophet Elijah worshipped the Lord (1 Kings 18). It has been kept in the Roman calendar since 1726. According to Carmelite tradition the Virgin Mary gave the scapular as a sign of her protection, and the Church sees in the scapular a sign of devotion to Mary and of a life lived in her care. In Kerala the Carmelite family is well known, and St Kuriakose Elias Chavara, who founded the Carmelites of Mary Immaculate, is honored in many parishes. Today’s Gospel fits Mary’s own way: she kept the feasts of her people faithfully, and her heart was full of mercy.
study: The Israelites ate the Passover “with sandals on the feet”, ready to leave. What am I being asked to leave behind in order to follow God?
Jesus answers a question about the sabbath with mercy. Is there a rule I keep strictly in my family or parish while forgetting the person it was made to serve?
